items.prompt: What does infrastructure as code (IaC) mean?

options.label: Configuring each server by hand and documenting the steps
Managing servers and networks through version-controlled code files
Writing application code that runs only on cloud servers
Storing server backups inside a source code repository

rubric: IaC defines infrastructure in code files kept under version control.
Distractors confuse IaC with app hosting, manual documentation or backups.

items.prompt: Which Terraform command previews the changes that would be made without changing any real resources?

options.label: `terraform plan`
`terraform destroy`
`terraform init`
`terraform apply`

rubric: `terraform plan` shows a preview only.
`apply` and `destroy` change real resources; `init` only prepares the directory.

items.prompt: In Terraform, what is the name of the data file that records which real resources it manages?

options.label: Module
Provider block
State file
Variable file

rubric: The state file maps configuration to real resources.
Other options are config constructs, not the record of managed resources.

items.prompt: A declarative IaC configuration primarily describes which of the following?

options.label: The history of every change made by staff
The exact ordered commands to run on each server
The logins of people allowed to edit the files
The desired end state of the infrastructure

rubric: Declarative code states what should exist, and the tool works out the steps.
The ordered commands option describes the imperative style.

items.prompt: In AWS CloudFormation, what is the file that describes the resources to create called?

options.label: Runbook
Snapshot
Template
Stack

rubric: A template defines the resources.
A stack is the deployed set of resources created from a template, not the file.

items.prompt: Which of the following are infrastructure as code tools? Select all that apply.

options.label: Terraform
Photoshop
Pulumi
AWS CloudFormation
Wireshark

rubric: Terraform, Pulumi and CloudFormation define infrastructure in code.
Wireshark analyses network traffic and Photoshop edits images.

items.prompt: A new teammate clones a repository containing Terraform files and opens a terminal in that folder. Nothing has been run there before. They are told to run `terraform init` first. What does this command do?

options.label: Creates all the cloud resources in the configuration
Uploads the local files to the cloud provider account
Downloads required providers and prepares the working directory
Deletes any resources not listed in the configuration

rubric: `init` downloads providers and sets up the working directory.
Creating or deleting resources is done by `apply`, not `init`.

items.prompt: You run `terraform apply` on a configuration, then run it again immediately with no code changes. What should happen the second time?

options.label: The command fails because the state is already used
Duplicate copies of every resource are created
No changes are made because infrastructure already matches
Every resource is destroyed and rebuilt from scratch

rubric: IaC tools are idempotent: matching state means no changes.
Distractors assume apply always recreates or duplicates resources.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to keep IaC files in a Git repository?

options.label: It keeps the real servers from being changed by hand
It keeps a reviewable history so changes can be traced and rolled back
It removes the need to run a plan before applying
It lets the cloud provider build resources faster

rubric: Git provides history, review and rollback of infrastructure changes.
Git does not speed up provisioning, replace plans or block manual console changes.

items.prompt: Why should you avoid writing a database password directly in a committed IaC file?

options.label: Terraform cannot read values written as plain text
Long passwords slow the plan because of file size
Anyone with repository access could read it from the file and history
The cloud provider rejects passwords that appear in code

rubric: Committed secrets are visible to all repo readers and persist in history.
The other options invent technical limits that do not exist.

items.prompt: A colleague changes a server's size in the cloud console by hand, and the code is unchanged. What will the next `terraform plan` most likely show?

options.label: No differences, since the console is the source of truth
A difference between the code and real server, proposing to revert
The code being rewritten to match the console change
An error saying the console cannot be used with Terraform

rubric: Drift is detected by comparing the code and state to reality, and plan proposes to restore the declared state.
Terraform never edits your code files automatically.

items.prompt: Which description best matches a declarative IaC definition?

options.label: A checklist of console clicks for an operator to follow
A scheduled job that retries failed commands every hour
A resource block stating a server with a given size and image
A shell script that runs create commands one after another

rubric: A declarative block states what should exist, not the steps.
The other options describe step-by-step or manual procedures.

items.prompt: Why is reviewing the output of `terraform plan` before applying valuable? Select all that apply.

options.label: It shows the effect of a code change without making it
It lets reviewers catch an accidental deletion before it happens
It previews which resources will be created, changed or destroyed
It guarantees the apply will not fail
It removes the need for a state file

rubric: Plan previews changes so reviewers can catch mistakes safely.
It cannot guarantee success and does not replace the state file.

items.prompt: An engineer renames a setting on a database resource in Terraform. The plan output marks the database with `-/+` and the note "must be replaced". What does this tell the engineer?

options.label: The database will only be removed from the state file
The database will be deleted and recreated, risking data loss
The database will be updated in place with no downtime
The plan has failed and nothing can be applied

rubric: `-/+` means destroy and recreate, which can lose data unless backed up.
It is not an in-place update or a plan error.

items.prompt: What does it mean that a tool such as Terraform or CloudFormation is declarative?

options.label: You describe the desired end state and the tool works out the steps to reach it
You declare only names of resources that were already built in the console
You write configuration in a language that has no variables or loops
You list each command in order and the tool runs them top to bottom

rubric: Declarative means specifying the target state, not the procedure.
The first distractor describes an imperative script.

items.prompt: Why does Terraform keep a state file?

options.label: To store a backup copy of the application source code for deployment
To map resources in the config to real resources so differences can be computed
To record who ran each command so that audits can assign blame later
To cache provider downloads so later runs start faster on any machine

rubric: State links config addresses to real resource IDs so plan can diff.
Caching and audit logging are not its purpose.

items.prompt: A configuration was applied successfully and nothing was changed in the code or in the cloud. What should applying it again do?

options.label: Duplicate each resource, since apply always adds new copies of them
Recreate every resource so that the environment is guaranteed fresh
Fail with an error, because a config can only be applied once safely
Make no changes, because the real state already matches the config

rubric: Declarative tools are idempotent: matching state means no changes.
Distractors assume apply is a one-shot imperative script.

items.prompt: In infrastructure as code, what is configuration drift?

options.label: Slow growth in the size of the config files as more resources are added
A provider upgrade that quietly renames resource types in the config
Real resources differing from the config because of changes made outside the code
The delay between running plan and running apply on the same config

rubric: Drift is divergence between actual infrastructure and the declared code, often from manual edits.
Other options confuse drift with file growth or timing.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of storing infrastructure code in Git rather than only changing resources in a console?

options.label: Cloud providers charge less for resources that are defined in a repository
Console access is no longer needed for any cloud account whatsoever
Resources are created faster because Git sends them directly to the cloud
Changes are reviewed, tracked in history and can be reverted from code

rubric: Version control gives review, history and rollback of infrastructure changes.
Git does not reduce cost or create resources itself.

items.prompt: Which are benefits of defining infrastructure as code? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each change leaves a history showing what changed and when
Changes can be peer reviewed in pull requests before being applied
Testing is no longer necessary because code never has mistakes
Identical environments can be recreated from the same files
Manual console edits automatically become part of the code

rubric: Reproducibility, review and history are core benefits.
Code can still be wrong, and console edits cause drift rather than updating code.

items.prompt: A teammate opens the cloud console and adds a new inbound rule to a security group that Terraform manages. The next day you run `terraform plan` without changing any code, and it shows one change on that security group. What best explains the plan output?

options.label: The state file was deleted overnight, so Terraform wants to rebuild the group
The real group differs from the config, so plan proposes restoring the declared rules
The plan always proposes changes to security groups on every single run
Terraform found a bug in the provider and wants to upgrade the group

rubric: Plan refreshes real state, sees drift and proposes reverting to the code.
Distractors invent provider bugs or state loss without evidence.

items.prompt: You have just written a new Terraform configuration in an empty directory and have not run any commands yet. Which command should you run first?

options.label: `terraform destroy`
`terraform apply -auto-approve`
`terraform refresh`
`terraform init`

rubric: init downloads providers and sets up the backend before plan or apply.
Apply and destroy cannot work before initialisation.

items.prompt: A config creates web servers with `count = 3` and all three exist already. You change it to `count = 5` and run `terraform plan`. What summary do you expect?

options.label: Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
Plan: 0 to add, 3 to change, 0 to destroy
Plan: 5 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy

rubric: Only the two missing instances are created; existing ones match.
Other options assume everything is rebuilt or add the wrong number.

items.prompt: Which snippet correctly defines an input variable named `region` with a default value in Terraform?

options.label: `variable = region("us-east-1")`
`variable "region" { default = "us-east-1" }`
`input "region" { value = "us-east-1" }`
`var region = "us-east-1"`

rubric: Variables use a variable block with an optional default argument.
The others use invented or incorrect syntax.

items.prompt: A subnet resource needs the ID of a VPC declared as `resource "aws_vpc" "main" {}`. Which line inside the subnet block passes it correctly?

options.label: `vpc_id = var.aws_vpc.main`
`vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id`
`vpc_id = main.aws_vpc.id`
`vpc_id = "aws_vpc.main.id"`

rubric: References use type.name.attribute and create a dependency.
A quoted string is literal text, and the other forms are the wrong order or namespace.

items.prompt: A config defines a storage bucket resource that already exists in state. You delete that resource block from the code and run `terraform apply`. What happens by default?

options.label: The bucket is renamed with a suffix and kept as a backup copy
Terraform asks you to rewrite the block before it will continue
The plan proposes destroying the bucket, since it is no longer declared
The bucket is left alone and removed only from the code

rubric: Resources in state but absent from config are planned for destruction.
Terraform does not keep undeclared resources unless they are removed from state.

items.prompt: You are preparing the first commit for a Terraform project. Which items should be kept out of the Git repository? Select all that apply.

options.label: The `.terraform.lock.hcl` dependency lock file
The local `terraform.tfstate` file, which can hold secrets
The `.tf` files that define the resources
A plaintext database password written inside a `.tf` file
The `.terraform` directory of downloaded provider plugins

rubric: State, secrets and downloaded plugins should not be committed.
The code and lock file should be committed for reproducibility.

items.prompt: Three teammates each run `terraform apply` from their laptops, each with a local state file. Yesterday two applies overlapped and one person's resources were duplicated. You need to prevent conflicting and duplicated applies. What should you do?

options.label: Delete the local state before each apply so every run starts clean
Commit the state file to Git and merge it when conflicts appear
Configure a shared remote backend that supports state locking
Let one person apply from a laptop and the others copy that state

rubric: A remote backend with locking gives one shared state and blocks concurrent applies.
Deleting or hand-merging state causes duplicates or lost tracking.

items.prompt: A teammate must apply exactly the changes you reviewed in a pull request, even if the config or remote resources change later. Which command sequence guarantees that?

options.label: `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan`
`terraform refresh` then `terraform apply`, since refresh records the reviewed changes
`terraform validate` then `terraform apply`, since validation locks the reviewed changes
`terraform plan` then `terraform apply -auto-approve`, since both read the same config

rubric: A saved plan file is applied exactly as reviewed.
Distractors assume a fresh plan, validate or refresh pins the changes; none of them do.

items.prompt: Subnets are created with `count = length(var.names)` from the list ["a","b","c"]. You then remove "b" from the list. What happens, and what avoids it?

options.label: Only subnet b is destroyed, because count tracks each name automatically
Subnet c shifts to index 1 and is replaced; `for_each` keyed by name avoids this
Nothing changes, because count ignores the contents of the list entirely
All subnets are recreated; adding `depends_on` to each subnet avoids this

rubric: count addresses resources by index, so removing a middle item shifts later ones; for_each keys by name.
Distractors assume count tracks names or that depends_on affects addressing.

items.prompt: `variables.tf` sets the default of `instance_type` to `t3.micro`, `terraform.tfvars` sets it to `t3.small`, and you run `terraform apply -var='instance_type=t3.large'`. Which size is used?

options.label: None; the command errors on conflicting values
`t3.large`
`t3.small`
`t3.micro`

rubric: Command-line -var has higher precedence than tfvars files and defaults.
Choosing t3.small assumes the file wins; the error option assumes conflicts are not resolved by precedence.

items.prompt: Which configuration makes Terraform create a VPC before its subnet without using `depends_on`?

options.label: The subnet block is written below the VPC block in the same file
The subnet sets `vpc_id = "vpc-main"` and the VPC is named `main`
The subnet and VPC share identical `tags` block values
The subnet sets `vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id`

rubric: Referencing an attribute of another resource creates an implicit dependency.
File order, names and tags do not affect the dependency graph.

items.prompt: You must pass a database password into a Terraform config without committing it to Git. Which approach does that?

options.label: Set a default in `variables.tf` and add that file to `.gitignore` afterwards
Base64-encode the password in `terraform.tfvars` and commit that file to the repo
Hardcode it in the resource block, since state files are stored encrypted anyway
Declare it with `sensitive = true` and supply it through a `TF_VAR_db_password` secret in CI

rubric: Environment-variable injection from a secret store keeps the value out of version control.
Distractors keep the secret in history or treat encoding or later ignoring as protection.

items.prompt: Your team of five shares one Terraform config on AWS. Which setup steps make the state safe to share? Select all that apply.

options.label: Restrict write access to the state bucket to the CI role and a few admins
Commit `terraform.tfstate` to Git so everyone has the latest copy
Enable versioning and encryption on the state bucket
Store state in a remote backend such as S3 with locking enabled
Give each engineer a separate local state file for the same resources

rubric: Remote, locked, versioned, encrypted and access-controlled state is the standard shared setup.
Committing state or using separate local states causes leaks, conflicts and divergence.

items.prompt: A load balancer was created by hand in the console. You want Terraform to manage it without recreating it, and you have already written a matching `aws_lb` resource block. What should you do next?

options.label: Add `lifecycle { ignore_changes = all }` so Terraform never touches the existing one
Import it into state with `terraform import` or an `import` block, then run `plan` to check differences
Delete the load balancer so Terraform can create it fresh from the block
Run `terraform apply`; Terraform finds the existing load balancer by name and adopts it

rubric: Existing resources must be imported into state; a follow-up plan reveals config mismatches.
Distractors assume auto-adoption, accept downtime, or hide the resource instead of managing it.

items.prompt: A plan shows `aws_instance.web must be replaced`, with `# forces replacement` beside `ami`. The only edit was bumping the AMI id. What explains this?

options.label: The instance has drifted, so Terraform replaces it to match the config
Terraform replaces any resource whose config file was edited
The state file is corrupt, so Terraform rebuilds whatever it cannot read
The provider cannot change `ami` in place, so the instance is destroyed and recreated

rubric: Some attributes are immutable, and the plan marks them as forcing replacement.
Distractors blame any edit, corruption or drift rather than the specific attribute.

items.prompt: Someone opened port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 in the console on a managed security group. The next `terraform plan` shows one in-place change removing that rule. What does this show?

options.label: Plan compares refreshed real state with config, so apply will revert the manual change
Terraform cannot see console edits, so this change comes from a code diff
The config is wrong and should be edited to match the console
The state file was edited, so Terraform is repairing the state first

rubric: Plan refreshes real resources and diffs them against config, revealing drift.
Distractors misread drift as a code change or a state edit.

items.prompt: A CI job was cancelled mid-apply. The next run fails with `Error acquiring the state lock`, showing a lock ID created two hours ago. What is the most likely cause and safe response?

options.label: Credentials expired, so rerun with `-lock=false` to bypass the check
A teammate's plan is running, so wait for the lock to expire on its own
A stale lock from the killed run; confirm nothing is applying, then `terraform force-unlock <ID>`
The state is corrupted, so delete it and re-import every resource

rubric: Killed runs leave locks; verify no active run before force-unlocking.
Disabling locking or deleting state risks concurrent writes or lost state.

items.prompt: `terraform plan` reports `Error: Cycle`. Security group `app` has an inline ingress rule referencing group `db`, and `db` has an inline ingress rule referencing `app`. What is the best fix?

options.label: Add `depends_on` to each group pointing at the other group
Apply each group separately with `-target` and keep the inline rules
Move the rules into separate `aws_security_group_rule` resources so both groups exist first
Set `count = 0` on one group until the other has been created

rubric: Inline cross-references make a circular graph; separate rule resources break the cycle.
depends_on adds edges rather than removing them; count and -target are fragile workarounds.

items.prompt: After a staging apply, a production database was destroyed. Both environments use the same backend bucket and key `app/terraform.tfstate`, with different variable files. What is the root cause?

options.label: Different variable files cannot configure different regions or accounts safely
The bucket lacked versioning, which is what triggered the deletion of the database
Terraform destroys resources whenever the variable file changes between runs
The shared state key made staging's run manage prod resources and plan their removal

rubric: One state shared by two environments means each run sees the other's resources as its own.
Versioning helps recovery but does not cause deletion; var files alone do not trigger destroys.

items.prompt: A CI plan showed 2 changes, but the later apply made 5. Which could explain the difference? Select all that apply.

options.label: Provider versions were not pinned, so a newer provider ran at apply
Apply ran a fresh plan instead of using the saved plan file
A teammate changed the config on the branch between plan and apply
The config had been formatted with `terraform fmt`
The state backend was encrypted

rubric: Unsaved plans, changed config and floating provider versions all let apply diverge from plan.
Encryption and formatting do not change planned actions.

items.prompt: You refactor `aws_db_instance.main` into a module called `database`. The plan now shows destroying `aws_db_instance.main` and creating `module.database.aws_db_instance.main`. What explains this and what is the fix?

options.label: It is a provider bug; set `ignore_changes = all` on the new database and apply
The plan is stale; run `terraform refresh` so the addresses are matched up
Modules always recreate their resources; keep databases outside modules
The resource address changed, so state sees the old gone and the new missing; add a `moved` block

rubric: State tracks resources by address; a moved block maps old to new without recreation.
Distractors blame modules, stale state or provider bugs instead of the address change.

items.prompt: After you rename a resource block label from `aws_db_instance.main` to `aws_db_instance.primary` with no other edits, `terraform plan` shows one destroy and one create. What explains this?

options.label: A stale state lock made Terraform treat every resource in the configuration as brand new
The label is an immutable attribute in the cloud API, so any change to it forces replacement
State tracks resources by address, so the old address looks removed and the new one looks added
The provider found drift in the live database and now forces a replacement to restore it

rubric: Resource addresses are the key into state; a `moved` block or `state mv` preserves the mapping.
Distractors blame drift or API immutability, but a label is a Terraform-only name.

items.prompt: Two engineers each keep a local `terraform.tfstate` committed to Git. Engineer A applies and pushes. Engineer B, who has not pulled, applies and tries to create the same load balancer again. What is the root cause?

options.label: The provider caches resource IDs per machine, and B's cache expired, forcing a duplicate create
Terraform refuses to read state older than the cloud resources, so it falls back to empty state
Git merges corrupt the state file's JSON structure, so Terraform can no longer parse any resource
B's state copy lacks A's resources, so B's plan assumes they do not exist and tries to create them

rubric: Divergent state copies cause duplicate creates; remote state with locking prevents this.
Distractors invent parsing or caching problems; the issue is stale state.

items.prompt: An apply fails with `DependencyViolation` while deleting a security group still used by an instance. The instance's config sets `vpc_security_group_ids = ["sg-0abc123"]` as a literal string. What is the faulty step?

options.label: The instance should use `count`, because a single instance cannot be detached from its group
The literal ID gives Terraform no dependency edge, so it may delete the group before updating the instance
The security group needs a `lifecycle` block, because groups can never be deleted while instances exist
The provider caches group IDs and so deletes in alphabetical order rather than dependency order

rubric: Referencing `aws_security_group.x.id` creates an implicit dependency that orders operations.
Distractors point at lifecycle or provider ordering, not the missing reference.

items.prompt: An autoscaling group has `desired_capacity = 3` in code. A scaling policy changes the live value during the day, and every morning `terraform plan` shows a diff back to 3. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: Two controllers own the same attribute: the code and the autoscaler, so each run sees drift from the autoscaler
The provider is buggy and miscalculates capacity, so a version upgrade alone would remove the diff
The scaling policy was created outside the code, so Terraform must destroy it before planning
The state backend is losing writes at night, so Terraform forgets the real capacity before each plan

rubric: Attributes managed at runtime should be excluded, for example with `ignore_changes`.
Distractors blame state or provider rather than dual ownership.

items.prompt: A config creates subnets with `count = length(var.cidrs)` and `cidr_block = var.cidrs[count.index]`. Removing the first CIDR from the list makes the plan replace every remaining subnet. Why?

options.label: `count` addresses resources by position, so the remaining items shift indexes and map to different state entries
Subnet CIDR blocks are tracked globally, so removing one invalidates all CIDRs in the same VPC
Terraform always replaces all resources in a set when its length changes, regardless of the meta-argument
The `length` function forces a data source refresh, which marks every dependent resource as tainted

rubric: Index-based addressing shifts; `for_each` with stable keys avoids this.
Distractors claim blanket replacement or taint, which does not happen.

items.prompt: A plan right after a successful apply, with no code change, shows pending changes. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: A data source looks up the latest AMI and now returns a newer image
`terraform fmt` reformatted the files, which counts as a resource change
The provider normalises a JSON policy differently from the string written in code
The backend stores state in an encrypted bucket, which hides some attributes
Another process, such as a console edit or an agent, changed a managed attribute

rubric: Moving data sources, external edits and normalisation differences all produce post-apply diffs.
Backend encryption and formatting do not affect planned resource changes.

items.prompt: A pipeline runs `terraform plan` on each pull request and `terraform apply -auto-approve` on merge. A reviewer approved a PR whose plan showed two tag changes. After merge, the apply also destroyed a database. Another PR had merged minutes earlier and removed that database's block. What is the root cause?

options.label: The merge-time apply computed a fresh plan against newer code and state, so it differed from the reviewed plan
The auto-approve flag makes Terraform ignore `prevent_destroy` and delete resources absent from the plan
The reviewer misread the plan, because tag changes always imply a replacement of attached resources
Terraform plans are nondeterministic, so two plans of identical code often disagree on destroys

rubric: Applying a saved plan file, or serialising merges, ensures the executed change matches the reviewed one.
Distractors blame the reviewer or nondeterminism instead of the plan/apply gap.

items.prompt: Criteria: a bad change in one service must not endanger others, teams deploy independently, and the shared network changes rarely. Which state layout best fits?

options.label: One state per individual resource, so every change has the smallest possible blast radius
Separate states per environment and component layer, sharing the network through read-only outputs
One state per environment containing everything, so all dependencies resolve within a single plan
One shared state across environments, with workspaces to separate dev from prod at apply time

rubric: Layered states limit blast radius while keeping the number of states manageable.
A monolithic state couples teams; per-resource states make dependencies unmanageable.

items.prompt: Criteria: no database password in Git, and no plaintext password in Terraform state if avoidable. Which approach best meets both?

options.label: Generate it with `random_password` and output it, so teammates can read it from the plan
Let the database service generate and rotate the admin secret in a secrets manager, never passing it through Terraform
Commit the password in an encrypted variables file and decrypt it during each pipeline run
Mark the password variable `sensitive = true` and pass it with `TF_VAR_db_password` from CI secrets

rubric: Service-managed secrets never enter the Terraform workflow, so they stay out of state.
`sensitive` only hides CLI output; the value still lands in state.

items.prompt: A reviewer sees a module that wraps `aws_s3_bucket` and exposes every argument as a variable, one to one, with no defaults or policies. Judged on maintainability and reuse, what is the best critique?

options.label: It adds indirection without encoding any standard, so it should either enforce conventions or be dropped
It is acceptable, but only if the module is stored in a separate repository from its callers
It should be split into one module per argument, so each setting is independently versioned
It is ideal, because exposing every argument guarantees callers never need to edit the module

rubric: A module earns its keep by encapsulating decisions such as encryption defaults and naming.
Pass-through wrappers add cost without abstraction; repo location is irrelevant.

items.prompt: Criterion: rank by irreversible impact if applied unnoticed. Which plan line deserves the closest review?

options.label: A new security group added, with no attachments to any resource yet
Tags updated in place on forty instances across two availability zones
An IAM policy description changed in place on a role used by one batch job
`aws_db_instance.orders` must be replaced, with no final snapshot configured

rubric: Replacing a stateful database without a snapshot can cause unrecoverable data loss.
The others are in-place, additive or easily reverted.

items.prompt: Criteria: engineers sometimes make emergency console fixes during incidents; changes must not be silently reverted, and every deviation must be auditable. Which drift policy fits best?

options.label: Adding `ignore_changes = all` to every resource, so drift never appears in any plan
An hourly auto-apply that restores code-defined state, so the repository is always authoritative
Scheduled plan-only runs that alert on drift, then reconcile by updating code or importing the change
Blocking all console access, so emergency fixes must go through a full pipeline run

rubric: Detect-and-review keeps incident fixes while preserving an audit trail.
Auto-apply can undo an emergency fix; blanket ignore hides drift entirely.

items.prompt: Criteria for a production pipeline: changes are reviewed before execution, risky changes are blocked automatically, and no long-lived cloud keys exist. Which controls satisfy these? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep a shared admin access key in CI variables, rotated yearly
Require approval of a saved plan file, then apply exactly that file
Authenticate the runner with short-lived OIDC-issued credentials
Run policy-as-code checks against the plan, failing on forbidden changes
Let engineers apply from laptops when the pipeline is slow

rubric: Saved-plan approval, policy checks and short-lived credentials map to the three criteria.
Long-lived shared keys and laptop applies break the credential and review criteria.

items.prompt: Thirty services each copy-paste the same VPC-and-ECS Terraform code. A security fix must reach all of them within two weeks, with the ability to roll back per service and reproducible plans. Which approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: Point every service at the module's `main` branch, so the fix reaches all of them on the next run
Move all thirty services into one root configuration, so one apply updates every service together
Publish a versioned module, pin each service to a tag, and roll out the fix as per-service version bumps
Keep the copies and send a patch file, since each service owner knows their own configuration

rubric: Pinned versions give staged rollout, per-service rollback and reproducible plans.
Tracking `main` makes plans non-reproducible; a monolith removes per-service rollback.

items.prompt: 40 engineers manage dev, staging and prod with Terraform. Criteria: no concurrent state corruption, small blast radius, and per-environment access control. Which state layout is best?

options.label: One shared state for all environments with locking, so every change sees the full picture
State files committed to Git per branch, since Git history gives versioning and peer review
Separate remote states per environment and component, each with locking and its own access policy
Local state on each engineer's laptop, synced by hand, so no shared backend is required

rubric: Splitting state by environment and component limits blast radius and allows separate access control, while locking prevents concurrent writes.
A single shared state widens blast radius; Git-stored state has no locking and exposes secrets.

items.prompt: On-call engineers sometimes hotfix resources in the console during incidents. Criteria: keep code as the source of truth, avoid surprise overwrites of valid fixes, and keep visibility. Which policy is best?

options.label: Run scheduled plan-only drift detection that alerts, then reconcile each diff in a reviewed code change
Run a scheduled apply every hour so any console change is overwritten and code always wins
Block all console write access permanently so drift can never occur, even during incidents
Add ignore_changes for every attribute so Terraform never reports differences from manual edits

rubric: Plan-only detection surfaces drift without overwriting valid emergency fixes, and reconciliation through code keeps the source of truth.
Auto-apply can undo an incident fix; ignore_changes hides drift entirely.

items.prompt: Thirty teams consume a shared network module. Criteria: reproducible plans, controlled upgrades, and visible impact of each change. Which sourcing approach is best?

options.label: Copy the module into each repository so teams can edit it freely without any upstream releases
Reference the module's main branch so every team receives fixes automatically on its next plan
Use a loose range such as >= 1.0 so plans stay current while remaining roughly compatible
Pin an exact released version and upgrade through a pull request that shows the resulting plan

rubric: Exact pins make plans reproducible, and upgrades via reviewed PRs make impact visible.
Tracking main or open ranges lets upstream changes alter plans unexpectedly; copies diverge.

items.prompt: A teammate says marking a database password variable `sensitive = true` keeps the secret safe in Terraform. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: It only hides the value in CLI output; plaintext still lands in state, so state needs encryption and tight access
Incorrect, because sensitive variables are written to plan output, which is the only place they are exposed
Correct, provided the variable is supplied from a .tfvars file that is excluded from Git commits
Correct, because sensitive values are stored encrypted in state and cannot be read by anyone with state access

rubric: The sensitive flag only redacts display; the value is still stored in plaintext in state.
Distractors assume state encryption or Git exclusion solves exposure.

items.prompt: A config creates one subnet per entry in a list of five names using `count`. Someone removes the second name. Criteria: no unintended destroys and readable diffs. Which assessment and fix is best?

options.label: Later entries shift index and get replaced; use for_each keyed by stable names so removal affects only one
Only the removed entry is destroyed, so count is safe here and the design needs no change at all
Shifted indexes are harmless because names are just tags; add create_before_destroy to avoid any outage
Count cannot accept lists, so the plan fails; wrap each name in a separate module call to fix it

rubric: Count addresses by index, so removing a middle item shifts and replaces later ones; for_each uses stable keys.
Distractors wrongly treat index shifts as harmless or count as invalid.

items.prompt: A team wants a production apply gate it can trust. Which practices make the gate reliable? Select all that apply.

options.label: Apply the exact saved plan file that reviewers approved, rather than re-planning at apply time
Run plan and apply with the same pinned tool and provider versions against the same backend
Let apply run a fresh plan automatically so it always reflects the newest cloud state
Have reviewers read only the code diff, since plan output merely repeats the same information
Highlight destroy and replace actions in the plan for explicit reviewer sign-off

rubric: Applying the reviewed plan, flagging destructive actions and keeping versions consistent ensure what is approved is what runs.
Code diffs do not show real effects, and a fresh plan at apply may differ from what was approved.

items.prompt: A refactor moves an aws_db_instance into a module, changing its address from aws_db_instance.main to module.data.aws_db_instance.main. The production plan shows one destroy and one create, with no attribute changes. Criteria: no data loss and no downtime. What is the best next step?

options.label: Taint the old address so Terraform treats the module copy as the same database on the next run
Add a moved block from the old address to the new one and confirm the plan then shows no changes
Apply with -target on the new address first so the database exists before the old one is destroyed
Apply after taking a snapshot, since restoring from it is an acceptable recovery for a destroyed database

rubric: A moved block remaps state to the new address so nothing is destroyed or recreated.
Snapshots and restore still cause downtime; -target or taint do not map identity.

items.prompt: Design a pipeline applying Terraform to dev, staging and prod accounts. Constraints: no long-lived cloud credentials stored, identical code in every environment, manual approval before prod. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Shared modules and one admin access key held in CI secrets, with an approval step added before the prod job
Shared modules applied from engineer laptops using personal credentials, with approval recorded in a ticket
Per-environment copies of the code, with access keys stored as CI secrets and rotated every ninety days
Shared modules, per-environment state, CI assuming per-account roles via OIDC, and an approval gate before prod

rubric: OIDC role assumption gives short-lived credentials, shared modules keep code identical, and a gate covers prod.
Stored keys, even rotated, violate the credential constraint; copies break identical code.

items.prompt: Design a change so replacing an instance group behind a load balancer causes no downtime. The group's name must be unique and cannot be changed in place. Which design meets both constraints?

options.label: Leave default ordering with a fixed name; the old group is destroyed, then the new one is created quickly
Use ignore_changes on the name and edit instances by hand so Terraform never needs to replace the group
Set create_before_destroy and keep a fixed name, so the new group takes over the old one in place
Set create_before_destroy and derive the name from a prefix or random suffix so old and new coexist

rubric: Creating the new group first needs a distinct name, so a prefix or suffix avoids the uniqueness conflict.
A fixed name with create_before_destroy fails on conflict; default ordering causes downtime.

items.prompt: Plan the adoption of 40 hand-built resources into Terraform. Constraints: no recreation, no downtime, and a way to verify that the code matches reality. Which plan meets them?

options.label: Delete the resources and apply fresh configuration in a short maintenance window to get clean state
Write matching configuration, import each resource into state, and iterate until the plan shows no changes
Write configuration from memory and apply it; Terraform will detect existing resources and adopt them
Copy a state file from a similar account and edit resource IDs by hand until the plan looks right

rubric: Import maps existing resources to state, and an empty plan verifies the code matches reality.
Recreation causes downtime; applying without import tries to create duplicates.

items.prompt: Design a control so no team can create a publicly readable storage bucket. Constraints: it must not rely on reviewers noticing, and it must also cover buckets created outside Terraform. Which design meets both?

options.label: A pull request checklist item reminding reviewers to reject public bucket settings in every change
Policy-as-code checks on the plan in CI, plus an organization-level control that blocks public access
A nightly script that lists public buckets and emails owners so they can fix them the next day
A module default of private access, which teams are trusted not to override in their own configs

rubric: CI policy checks automate prevention in code, and an org-level control covers console-created buckets.
Checklists, notifications and trusted defaults depend on people or only cover Terraform.

items.prompt: Plan how to split a 2,000-resource state into network, data and app states. Constraints: no resource recreated, short lock time, and the result must be verifiable. Which plan meets them?

options.label: Split only the configs and keep the single state in place, since states cannot be separated later
Create new configs, destroy resources in the old state, and apply the new configs to recreate them
Copy the full state into each new backend, then delete unwanted resources from each config afterward
Back up state, move each resource group to its new state, then confirm every state plans with no changes

rubric: Moving resources between states preserves identity, and empty plans in each state verify success.
Copying state duplicates ownership and deleting from config would destroy resources.

items.prompt: Design per-pull-request ephemeral environments with Terraform. Which elements must the design include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A per-environment state key and resource name suffix derived from the PR number to avoid collisions
Cost-limited sizing and quotas defined in the module so previews cannot exhaust the account budget
Manual cleanup by the author after merge, tracked in the PR description
Automatic destroy on PR close plus a TTL sweep for environments that were abandoned
A shared state file with fixed resource names so every PR updates the same environment

rubric: Isolated state and names prevent collisions, automated teardown prevents leaks, and limits control cost.
Shared state causes PRs to clobber each other; manual cleanup is routinely forgotten.

items.prompt: A module used by 30 teams has an input `vpc_cidr` that should become `network_cidr`, and the default of `enable_flow_logs` should change to true. Constraint: no team's plan may break or change unexpectedly when upgrading within its current major version. Which release design meets this?

options.label: Rename the input and flip the default in a patch release, announcing it in the changelog for teams to read
Publish a new module with the new names and delete the old one so teams are forced to migrate at once
Accept both inputs and keep the old default in a minor release with a deprecation notice, then switch the default in the next major
Rename the input and flip the default in a major release, trusting teams to pin versions before they upgrade

rubric: Supporting both inputs and keeping the default until a major release avoids breakage or surprise diffs within a major version.
Renames or default flips in patch or major releases, or deleting the module, break or alter existing plans.
